body.h2: Summary
body.text: 3 November 2020

body.h2: Summary
body.text: In our [Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/conditionsanddiseases/bulletins/coronaviruscovid19infectionsurveypilot/latest), the latest estimate shows the number of infections continues to increase. There has been growth in all age groups over the past two weeks in England; older teenagers and young adults continue to have the highest current rates, while rates appear to be steeply increasing among secondary school-aged children.

body.h2: Summary
body.text: An estimated 568,100 people had COVID-19 within the community population in England between 17 and 23 October 2020, equating to around 1 in 100 people. In Wales, an estimated 26,100 people had COVID-19 during the same period, equating to around 1 in 120 people. In Northern Ireland, during the same period, an estimated 24,300 had COVID-19, equating to 1 in 80 people. Our survey has been extended to Scotland, where in the most recent two weeks (10 to 23 October 2020) an estimated 37,400 people had COVID-19, equating to 1 in 140 people.

body.h2: Summary
body.text: We have also carried out [analysis](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/coronaviruscovid19infectionsurveycharacteristicsofpeopletestingpositiveforcovid19inenglandoctober2020) of the characteristics of people in the community who tested positive for the coronavirus (COVID-19) in England. Almost half of people who have tested positive for COVID-19 in the most recent fortnight have reported symptoms around the time of their test.

body.h2: Summary
body.text: All age groups have higher positivity rates in higher-rate regions in England, with 17- to 24-year-olds having the highest positivity rates in higher- and lower-rate regions.

body.h2: Summary
body.text: Urban areas in England are estimated to have higher positivity rates than rural areas. There is also no longer a difference in positivity rates between those travelling and not travelling abroad.

body.h2: Summary
body.text: The total number of deaths registered in England and Wales in the [week ending 23 October](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/birthsdeathsandmarriages/deaths/bulletins/deathsregisteredweeklyinenglandandwalesprovisional/latest) increased compared with the previous week, as did deaths involving the coronavirus (COVID-19). Despite rising to the highest since the week ending 12 June 2020, the number of COVID-19 deaths remained low compared with figures seen at the peak of the pandemic.

body.h2: Summary
body.text: View our summaries of the [economy](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/conditionsanddiseases/articles/coronaviruscovid19roundupeconomybusinessandjobs/2020-07-02), [social impacts](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/conditionsanddiseases/articles/coronaviruscovid19rounduppeopleandsocialimpacts/2020-07-03) or [go to our main roundup page for the latest across all topics](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/conditionsanddiseases/articles/coronaviruscovid19roundup/2020-03-26).

body.h2: Summary
body.text: This page is a summary of insights from our most recent analysis and will be updated as new publications are released. [Sign up to our email alerts for daily updates](https://public.govdelivery.com/accounts/UKONS/subscribers/new) in your inbox.

body.h2: Characteristics of people testing positive for coronavirus (COVID-19)
body.text: Analysis of the characteristics of people in the community who tested positive for the coronavirus (COVID-19) has shown a higher percentage of people reporting symptoms at or around the time of their test in recent weeks, compared with a low point in the summer months.

body.h2: Characteristics of people testing positive for coronavirus (COVID-19)
body.text: From 28 September to 11 October 2020, 34% of participants in the Office for National Statistics (ONS) Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey who tested positive for COVID-19 reported any evidence of symptoms at the time of the test. A smaller proportion of those who tested positive, 24%, reported experiencing a cough, fever or anosmia (loss of taste or smell) at the time of the test.

body.h2: Characteristics of people testing positive for coronavirus (COVID-19)
body.text: Overall, during late June to late July, very few people who tested positive reported any evidence of symptoms at the time of their positive test (as low as 0%), compared with up to 38% at other times.

body.h2: Monthly mortality analysis, September 2020
body.text: Monthly mortality analysis, September 2020

body.h2: Monthly mortality analysis, September 2020
body.text: Mortality rates for deaths in September 2020 due to the coronavirus (COVID-19) have increased for the first time since the peak in April 2020.

body.h2: Monthly mortality analysis, September 2020
body.text: [Our monthly mortality analysis](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/birthsdeathsandmarriages/deaths/bulletins/monthlymortalityanalysisenglandandwales/latest) of provisional death registration data in England and Wales in September 2020 shows there were 39,827 deaths registered in England, 2,568 deaths more than the five-year average for September; in Wales, there were 2,610 deaths registered, 135 deaths more than the five-year average.

body.h2: Monthly mortality analysis, September 2020
body.text: The leading cause of death in September 2020 was dementia and Alzheimer’s disease in England (accounting for 11.2% of all deaths) and in Wales (11.1% of all deaths). The coronavirus (COVID-19) did not feature in the top 10 leading causes of death in September 2020, neither in England nor in Wales.

body.h2: Monthly mortality analysis, September 2020
body.text: Age-standardised mortality rates (ASMRs) are used for comparisons over time rather than numbers of deaths, as ASMRs account for changes to the population size and age structure.

body.h2: Monthly mortality analysis, September 2020
body.text: The ASMR of deaths in September 2020 due to COVID-19 was 12.6 per 100,000 persons in England, and in Wales the ASMR was 10.8 per 100,000 persons; in England, for the first time since April 2020, the COVID-19 mortality rate [significantly](https://www.ons.gov.uk/methodology/methodologytopicsandstatisticalconcepts/uncertaintyandhowwemeasureit#statistical-significance) increased, compared with the previous month.

body.h2: Monthly mortality analysis, September 2020
body.text: Since September 2003, overall mortality rates in England for the month of September had been decreasing, to a low in September 2018. However, the overall mortality rate significantly increased in September 2019 and in September 2020. Mortality rates in Wales show a similar pattern over time.

body.h2: Deaths in private homes
body.text: We have provided [detailed analysis of deaths](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/deathsinprivatehomesenglandandwales) that occurred in private homes in England and Wales during the pandemic.

body.h2: Deaths in private homes
body.text: There were 108,842 deaths in private homes in England registered from 28 December 2019 to 11 September 2020, and 7,440 deaths in private homes in Wales in the same period.

body.h2: Deaths in private homes
body.text: This was 25,472 deaths more than the five-year average in England and 1,624 deaths more than the five-year average in Wales.

body.h2: Deaths in private homes
body.text: The number of deaths in private homes registered in England each week in 2020 was above the five-year average, with the exception of the week ending 3 January. In Wales, the number of deaths in private homes has remained above the five-year average since the week ending 20 March, with the exception of the week ending 4 September.

body.h2: Deaths in private homes
body.text: Males accounted for a higher percentage of excess deaths in private homes than females. People aged 70 to 89 years contributed most to the excess deaths in private homes, accounting for 58.5% of excess deaths in England and 63.6% in Wales.

body.h2: Deaths in private homes
body.text: Deaths in private homes for males from ischaemic heart diseases increased by 25.9% in England and 22.7% in Wales compared with the five-year average. Deaths in private homes for females from dementia and Alzheimer’s disease increased by 75.0% in England and 92.2% in Wales compared with the five-year average.

body.h2: Deaths in private homes
body.text: In England, between the week ending 20 March 2020 and the week ending 11 September 2020, 39.6% of all deaths occurred in hospitals, followed by private homes (27.7%) and care homes (25.9%). However, since the peak in deaths, trends have differed between places of death.

body.text: A substantial proportion of the [differences in COVID-19 mortality for people of ethnic minority backgrounds](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/explainingethnicbackgroundcontrastsindeathsinvolvingcovid19england2ndmarchto3rdjuly2020) can be explained by demographic, geographical and socioeconomic factors, modelling has found.

body.h2: Ethnic background contrasts in deaths involving COVID-19
body.text: After adjustments for those factors, males in all ethnic minority groups other than Chinese retained a higher rate of COVID-19 mortality; for females, all other than Bangladeshi, Chinese and Mixed ethnic groups retained a raised rate of COVID-19 mortality following adjustments.

body.h2: COVID-19 deaths compared with those from influenza and pneumonia
body.text: COVID-19 deaths compared with those from influenza and pneumonia

body.h2: COVID-19 deaths compared with those from influenza and pneumonia
body.text: More than three times as many people died due to the coronavirus (COVID-19) than influenza and pneumonia, between January and August 2020.

body.h2: COVID-19 deaths compared with those from influenza and pneumonia
body.text: Our [analysis of deaths in England and Wales](http://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/birthsdeathsandmarriages/deaths/bulletins/deathsduetocoronaviruscovid19comparedwithdeathsfrominfluenzaandpneumoniaenglandandwales/deathsoccurringbetween1januaryand31august2020) has shown that COVID-19 claimed the lives of 48,168 people, while 13,619 people died of pneumonia and 394 died from influenza.

body.h2: COVID-19 deaths compared with those from influenza and pneumonia
body.text: While influenza and pneumonia were mentioned on more death certificates between January and August 2020, COVID-19 was the underlying cause of death in more than three times as many deaths.

body.h2: COVID-19 deaths compared with those from influenza and pneumonia
COVID-19 deaths compared with those from influenza and pneumonia
body.chartbuilder_h3: There were more deaths due to COVID-19 between January and August 2020 than influenza or pneumonia
body.chartbuilder_h4: Number of deaths due to influenza, pneumonia or COVID-19 by sex, England and Wales, occurring between 1 January and 31 August 2020 and registered by 5 September 2020

body.h2: COVID-19 deaths compared with those from influenza and pneumonia
body.text: Between 1 January and 31 August 2020, there were 1.3 times as many deaths where influenza or pneumonia was a contributory factor than COVID-19, but COVID-19 was the underlying cause in 3.4 times as many deaths.

body.h2: COVID-19 deaths compared with those from influenza and pneumonia
body.text: In 2020 fewer people aged 85 years and older died of influenza and pneumonia compared with the five-year average, while the proportion of people in the same age group dying from COVID-19 was higher.

body.h2: COVID-19 deaths compared with those from influenza and pneumonia
body.text: The proportion of care home deaths due to COVID-19 was almost double that of deaths due to influenza and pneumonia (30.0% and 15.2% respectively).

body.h2: COVID-19 deaths compared with those from influenza and pneumonia
body.text: There were more COVID-19 deaths between 1 January and 31 August 2020 than influenza and pneumonia for the same period every year between 1959 and 2020.

body.h2: COVID-19 deaths compared with those from influenza and pneumonia
body.text: This article uses death occurrences (based on date a death occurred) rather than death registrations (based on date a death was registered), as occurrences are more useful in examining trends over time.

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by occupation
body.text: Deaths involving COVID-19 by occupation

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by occupation
body.text: Among men working in health care and social care, the rate of death involving the coronavirus (COVID-19) was around 3.2 times higher in those who likely acquired the virus before lockdown than those who likely acquired the virus during lockdown.

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by occupation
body.text: Between 9 March and 30 June 2020, prior to the widespread easing of lockdown restrictions, 5,330 deaths involving COVID-19 in the working age population (those aged 20 to 64 years) of England and Wales were registered. 72.0% of the total number (3,839 deaths) were likely to be a result of an infection acquired before lockdown on 23 March. Occupation information is available on the death certificate.

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by occupation
body.text: [Our analysis shows](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/coronaviruscovid19relateddeathsbyoccupationenglandandwalesbeforeandduringthelockdown) that mortality rates for both sexes during lockdown were generally half those seen before lockdown for all major occupation groups. Despite this, some groups of occupations continued to have high rates of death involving COVID-19 across the entire period, when compared to rates in the population.

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by occupation
body.text: Among men, four out of the nine major occupation groups had higher rates of death involving COVID-19 in the before and during lockdown groups, compared with rates among those of the same age and sex in the population (elementary occupations; caring, leisure and other service occupations; process, plant and machine operatives; and skilled trades occupations).

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by occupation
body.text: Among women, only those working in the caring, leisure and other service occupations had higher rates of death involving COVID-19 in the before and during lockdown groups. People working in the health and social care sector are recorded in a wide range of occupational groups. Men working in health and social care experienced rates of death involving COVID-19 that were three times higher in the before lockdown group than the during lockdown group. For women, only social care workers had elevated rates in the before lockdown group.

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by disability status
body.text: Deaths involving COVID-19 by disability status

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by disability status
body.text: Disabled people (those limited a little and those limited a lot in their day-to-day activities by a long-term health problem or disability) aged nine years and over made up almost 6 out of 10 COVID-19 deaths in England and Wales between 2 March and 14 July 2020. Amongst COVID-19 related deaths of females aged 65 years and over, the proportion made up by disabled people was largest, accounting for 67% of the total.

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by disability status
body.text: [Our analysis](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/birthsdeathsandmarriages/deaths/articles/coronaviruscovid19relateddeathsbydisabilitystatusenglandandwales/2marchto14july2020) shows that males and females aged 9 years and over who were disabled had higher age-standardised mortality rates (ASMR) than those who were non-disabled.

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by disability status
body.text: Males who were disabled and limited a lot in their day-to-day activities had an overall age-standardised COVID-19 mortality rate of 240.8 deaths per 100,000 (non-disabled: 84.2 deaths per 100,000). Females who were disabled had an age-standardised COVID-19 mortality rate of 169.9 deaths per 100,000 (non-disabled: 44.4 deaths per 100,000).

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by disability status
body.text: The relative gaps in ASMRs between disabled and non-disabled males and females were largest amongst those aged 9 to 64 years. Mortality rates for those aged 9 to 64 years who were disabled and limited a lot in their day-to-day activities were 10.8 times greater for females and 6.5 times greater for males, than for non-disabled people in the same age and sex group.

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by disability status
body.text: Adjusting for age, socio-demographic, geographic and household characteristics reduced the relative difference in mortality rates between the disabled and non-disabled. The relative difference in mortality rates between those who were disabled and limited a lot in their day-to-day activities and those non-disabled was 2.4 times higher for females and 2.0 times higher for males.

body.h2: Effect of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic on suicide unclear
body.text: Effect of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic on suicide unclear

body.h2: Effect of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic on suicide unclear
body.text: [Provisional data show there were 2,107 deaths by suicide](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/quarterlysuicidedeathregistrationsinengland2001to2019registrationsandquarter1jantomartoquarter2aprtojune2020provisionaldata) registered in England between January and June 2020. However, only one -fifth of these (21.6%) had a date of death that was also in 2020. This is because of the length of time it can take to hold an inquest into these deaths. As a result of this delay, we cannot yet be sure of the number of suicides that occurred during the coronavirus (COVID -19) pandemic.

body.h2: Effect of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic on suicide unclear
body.text: According to the data, there were 10.3 deaths by suicide per 100,000 people in Quarter 1 (Jan to Mar) 2020 , and 6.9 deaths by suicide per 100,000 people in Quarter 2 (Apr to June) 2020. The number of suicide registrations in Quarter 2 is 30% lower than the average number of registrations for the same period between 2015 and 2019, and is the lowest number of any quarter since 2001.

body.h2: Effect of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic on suicide unclear
body.text: However, these numbers should be interpreted with caution. It is likely that the lower number of suicides registered in this period reflects the impact of the coronavirus pandemic on coroner services in England and Wales, such as delays to inquests caused by services adapting to social distancing measures. It is unlikely that this decrease represents a genuine reduction in the number of suicides.

body.h2: Effect of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic on suicide unclear
body.text: The earliest date we will be able to more fully report on provisional data on suicide deaths during the coronavirus pandemic will be in 2021.

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by local area and socioeconomic deprivation
body.text: Deaths involving COVID-19 by local area and socioeconomic deprivation

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by local area and socioeconomic deprivation
body.text: We have published [provisional analysis of all deaths involving the coronavirus (COVID-19)](http://ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/birthsdeathsandmarriages/deaths/bulletins/deathsinvolvingcovid19bylocalareasanddeprivation/deathsoccurringbetween1marchand31july2020) that occurred in England and Wales between 1 March and 31 July 2020, (registered up to 15 August 2020), focusing on differences between local areas.

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by local area and socioeconomic deprivation
body.text: Our analysis shows that between March and July, there were 259,199 deaths occurring in England and Wales, 51,831 of which involved COVID-19 (20% of all deaths).

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by local area and socioeconomic deprivation
body.text: Over this period, there were 90.2 deaths involving COVID-19 per 100,000 people in England and Wales. Looking at both countries separately, this equates to 90.9 deaths per 100,000 people in England compared with 75.7 per 100,000 people in Wales.

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by local area and socioeconomic deprivation
body.text: Wales and all English regions recorded an increase in age-standardised mortality rates (ASMR) involving COVID-19 between March and April, followed by decreases in May through to July 2020. However, in England, for the month of July, the ASMR for deaths involving COVID-19 in the most deprived areas of the country was more than double that seen in the least deprived areas (3.1 deaths per 100,000 people compared with 1.4). This continued a theme seen in previous months.

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by local area and socioeconomic deprivation
body.text: Our analysis also shows that in July 2020, of the 336 local authority areas in England and Wales, 71 had no deaths in July involving COVID-19 and only two areas recorded more than 20 such deaths. These two areas were Leicester and Ashford, which saw 24 and 21 deaths involving COVID-19 respectively.
